metadata.title: For Claude, Not For You.
metadata.subtitle: The Command Development Skill
metadata.purpose: Take apart the slash-command file format: name what the body actually is (a directive TO Claude, not a message to the user), enumerate the levers the format exposes (three scopes, five frontmatter fields, two argument shapes, @ file refs, CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT), and judge the design choice that pushes the single most useful dynamic trick — inline shell calls — off the main page into a reference file. Land the carry-out that a command's body is written for Claude, not for you.

beats.narration_text: Here's the mistake worth catching. Someone read a command body and assumed it described what would happen to them. It doesn't — it's a directive TO Claude. The words are pointed at the model, not at the reader. So when I write a command body, am I writing it for Claude?

beats.narration_text: Here's what a slash command actually is. A Markdown file with a YAML header — nothing exotic. The body is a directive TO Claude, not a description of what the user will see. That file lives in one of three places: project commands, shared with the team and scoped to that project; personal commands, yours in every project; and plugin commands, bundled with an installed plugin. Same format, three scopes — they optimized for one uniform authoring surface at the cost of making you track where each command lives. The frontmatter carries five fields: description, allowed-tools, model, argument-hint, and disable-model-invocation. Five levers, no more.

production_viz.label: ANATOMY: LOCATIONS + FIELDS
production_viz.caption: scope, then the fields that shape it

beats.narration_text: Arguments come in two shapes. Dollar-ARGUMENTS grabs everything typed after the command as one string — coarse-grained, easy. Dollar-1, dollar-2 pick off individual pieces: a PR number in the first slot, a priority level in the second. The at-sign reads a file — at-dollar-1 opens whatever path the argument names; a static reference like at-package-dot-json embeds a known file every time, no argument needed. Plugin commands get one more lever: CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT resolves to the plugin's own folder, so a command can point at its own scripts without a hardcoded absolute path — that's the design choice that lets a plugin ship anywhere without knowing where it landed. One honest note from the skill itself: this whole file format is now considered legacy. New work is pointed toward a skill file instead. Learn it, but know you're learning a lever that's already been marked down.

production_viz.label: ARGUMENTS + FILE REFS
production_viz.caption: one string, or one piece at a time

beats.narration_text: One gap worth naming. A command can also run a shell command inline before Claude ever sees the rest of the body — an exclamation mark, then backticks, dropping something like the current git diff straight into the prompt. That's the single most useful dynamic trick the format has: your command can hand Claude live evidence instead of a stale description. Here's the design choice that costs you. The guide that teaches command-writing doesn't show this inline. It's pushed off into a separate reference file. They optimized the main page for the flat frontmatter fields at the expense of surfacing the one feature that turns commands from templates into pipelines. You find it only if you go looking.

production_viz.label: ONE GAP
production_viz.caption: not taught where you'd look for it

beats.narration_text: A slash command's body is written for Claude, not for you. The words that matter tell Claude what to do — not what you'll see happen.

props.sparkLine: Direct Claude. Don't describe the outcome.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: Design a Claude Code slash command called review-pr that takes a PR number as an argument, reads the changed files, and reviews them for code quality. Write it as a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter. In the body, address Claude directly as instructions — don't describe what the user will see. Use dollar-1 for the PR number and set the argument-hint field. Restrict allowed-tools to only what the command actually needs. Show the exclamation-mark backtick syntax inline for pulling in the PR diff automatically, instead of asking Claude to fetch it. Then explain, field by field, why each frontmatter choice matters. Watch four things: does the body direct Claude, or describe the user? Does it capture the PR number with dollar-1 and an argument-hint? Does allowed-tools narrow the surface? And does it drop the diff into the prompt with an inline shell call, or send you off to a reference file? Go deeper: ask the same model what changes if this becomes a plugin command instead of a project command — where does the file live, how does CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT rewrite the file references inside the body, and what breaks about the personal-command version the moment a teammate tries to use it?
